passage:
Monday, the week before Ganesh festival: The class decoration committee was really Urmila's group of five. When Keya from the group spilled glue across the big chart, Urmila laughed. "Accidents happen. Just cover it with glitter." Nilesh, who had been added to the committee late, said nothing and fetched a cloth.
Thursday: Nilesh stapled the paper lanterns a little crooked. "Who let him touch it?" Urmila said loudly. "This is why we don't take outsiders." The group giggled. Nilesh's ears burned, and he stapled the rest in silence.
The next Monday, after the festival: The class teacher praised the committee's work. Urmila's group went up to collect the certificate. Nilesh's name was on the list, but nobody called him. He stayed at his desk, straightening pencils that were already straight, remembering the glue that didn't matter and the staples that did.

qa.q: What did Keya spill on the chart?
qa.a: Glue, across the big chart.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when Urmila said "This is why we don't take outsiders"?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, his ears burning, because the same kind of small slip that was laughed off for Keya was used to shame him.

qa.q: How could the class teacher support Nilesh?
qa.a: The teacher could call every name on the committee list for the certificate, and set the same rules for mistakes for everyone, whichever group they belong to.

qa.q: Why might Urmila react so differently to Keya's glue and Nilesh's staples?
qa.a: Keya is inside Urmila's group, so her mistake feels like an accident, while Nilesh is an outsider, so his slip looks like proof he doesn't belong.

grounding: Shows a teenager outside a clique who sees its members excuse each other's mistakes while judging his harshly.

passage: The district cooperative dairy near Kolhapur took six interns that summer, and by the second week Kishore had noticed something. The supervisor, Patil saheb, gave the plant-floor work, the part that counted for jobs, to the three boys from his own taluka. Kishore was one of them. Sarita, who had topped the college and came from Nanded, was sent to file milk slips. When the lab needed an extra hand, Patil saheb said, "Kishore, you come, you're one of ours." When Sarita asked a question about fat testing, he said, "Ask later." Kishore felt the unfairness sit in his chest like a stone, even while he enjoyed the lab. That evening, walking to the bus stand, he said to Sarita, "I think the good work goes to people from his area. It isn't about you." Sarita stopped walking. "I thought I was imagining it."

qa.q: What work was Sarita given?
qa.a: She was sent to file milk slips.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling while he enjoyed the lab work?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a bit guilty, the unfairness sitting in his chest like a stone even though he was the one benefiting.

qa.q: What could Kishore do next, after naming the pattern?
qa.a: He could suggest to Patil saheb that plant-floor and lab tasks rotate among all six interns, and keep backing Sarita when she asks questions.

qa.q: How had Sarita been seeing her own treatment?
qa.a: Sarita had wondered whether she was imagining it, perhaps doubting herself, so hearing Kishore name the pattern was a relief.

grounding: Shows a student noticing that work and trust flow toward interns from the supervisor's own area, and naming the pattern as a first step toward fairness.

passage:
"Ishita, look at the last two on the list. I'm tempted to just pick Rhea."
"Because she's good?"
"Because she's from my old college, my department, knows my professors." Nikita laughed. "Which is exactly why I'm worried."
"So what do you want to do?"
"Use the sheet we agreed on. Portfolio, problem task, reference. Scores first, names after."
"And Farid? His portfolio was stronger than either of us expected."
"It was. Let me ask myself something. If Farid had come from my college with this same portfolio, would I hesitate?"
"Would you?"
"No. I'd call him tomorrow." Nikita tapped the sheet. "Also, we've hired four people from the same two colleges this year. Let's ask the polytechnic's placement cell to send candidates next round."
"I'll email them now. And you'll call Farid?"
"First thing in the morning."

qa.q: What three things are on the agreed sheet?
qa.a: Portfolio, problem task and reference.

qa.q: Why is Nikita worried about wanting to pick Rhea?
qa.a: Nikita feels a warm pull towards someone from her own college and department, and is uneasy that familiarity, not the work, is driving the choice.

qa.q: Which checks helped Nikita decide fairly?
qa.a: Scoring on the agreed sheet before names, asking whether she would hesitate if Farid came from her own college, and reaching out to a different college next round.

qa.q: How might Farid be affected by Nikita's method?
qa.a: Farid is judged on his strong portfolio rather than on where he studied, so he gets a call he might otherwise have missed.

grounding: Shows a colleague using clear criteria, seeking candidates unlike herself, and checking whether she would make the same call for someone from her own group.

passage:
Tuesday, the week before the Christmas holidays: Jatin had to stand outside the classroom in the cold corridor all through maths. Kishore watched through the window. "He must have been really naughty," he whispered to Ravi. "Sir doesn't punish good kids."
Wednesday: At recess Jatin sat alone on the steps. Kishore didn't sit with him. Amma always says good people get good things, he thought. So Jatin can't be good.
Friday: In assembly, the principal announced that the science lab window had been broken by a football from the senior ground, not by anyone in class five. Sir called Jatin to the front and said sorry in front of everyone. Kishore stared at his shoes. Jatin had stood in the cold for nothing, and Kishore had kept away.

qa.q: Where did Jatin have to stand on Tuesday?
qa.a: Outside the classroom in the cold corridor, all through maths.

qa.q: Why did Kishore feel sure Jatin had done something bad?
qa.a: Kishore believed good people get good things, so the punishment felt like proof; believing it made the world seem fair and safe to him.

qa.q: What could Kishore do after Friday's assembly?
qa.a: He could sit with Jatin at recess and say sorry for keeping away, and remember next time that a punishment can be a mistake.

qa.q: What was the week like for Jatin?
qa.a: Jatin was punished for something he didn't do and then left alone at recess, so the week was probably lonely and unfair until the apology.

grounding: Shows a child believing a punished classmate must have done something bad, because the world is supposed to be fair.

passage: Hrithik, you said your friend "asked for it" when those boys took his phone. Sit with me on the steps; the Holi colours can dry. When I was sixteen, a boy in my class, Sohan, was robbed on the canal road. They took his new watch and pushed him into the ditch. The headmaster phoned his father and the police that same evening. And do you know what I said the next day? "He must have been showing off that watch." I said it loudly, so everyone heard. The truth is, I walked that same canal road every day. If Sohan had done nothing wrong and still got hurt, then it could happen to me. Blaming him let me feel safe. Sohan heard me. He never walked home with us again. That is the Varun chacha story I'm not proud of.

qa.q: What was taken from Sohan on the canal road?
qa.a: His new watch; he was also pushed into the ditch.

qa.q: Why did young Varun blame Sohan for the robbery?
qa.a: Varun walked the same road every day, and believing Sohan had done something wrong let Varun feel safe instead of afraid that it could happen to him too.

qa.q: What choice in the story could young Varun have made differently?
qa.a: Instead of blaming Sohan loudly, he could have checked on Sohan and walked the canal road home with him.

qa.q: How might Sohan have felt hearing Varun's comment?
qa.a: Sohan probably felt hurt and ashamed on top of being robbed, which is why he never walked home with them again.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming a robbed classmate to protect the comfort of believing he himself is safe.

passage: Chinmay, eat the khapse first; it's Losar, no gloomy faces. Your mother told me what your hostel mates said about your illness, that it was somehow your own fault. Let me tell you what happened to Dolma at nineteen. I was in second year in Darjeeling when a long fever kept me in bed for three months. I missed my exams. An aunty at the monastery gate said it happened because I had been proud. A classmate said I had been careless. I started believing them. I stopped answering letters. I didn't even tell the professor why I had missed the exams; it felt like confessing a sin. Only my roommate, Pema, kept coming with tea and copied notes, and never once asked what I had done wrong. She is the reason I went back.

qa.q: How long did the fever keep Dolma in bed?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: Why did young Dolma stop answering letters?
qa.a: Being told the illness was deserved added shame to the pain, so Dolma felt guilty and withdrew into silence, as if missing exams were a sin to confess.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Dolma go back?
qa.a: Pema's choice to keep coming with tea and copied notes without asking what Dolma had done wrong, which gave support instead of blame.

qa.q: How did Pema see Dolma's illness?
qa.a: Pema treated it as misfortune that needed care, not as a punishment, and kept showing up with tea and notes.

grounding: Shows a student who fell ill and missed exams being told the illness was deserved, which added shame to the pain and pushed the student into silence.

passage: When the layoffs came last June, Sangeeta was on the list. She had trained half our team, including me. By lunch, someone in the pantry was saying, "There must be a reason. They don't cut good people." I felt the pull of that idea too; it's comforting to think the world only punishes mistakes. But I had seen her work. Sometimes a whole project gets cut, and the best person on it goes with it. So I didn't try to explain it. I sat with her on the office steps while she cried, then helped her pack her plants. She hugged me and said, "Ankita, you didn't have to." That evening I wrote her a detailed reference. The next week I asked our manager, in writing, why the layoff criteria hadn't been shared, and three colleagues signed with me. We got the criteria in July. It didn't bring Sangeeta back, but the next list came with reasons.

qa.q: What did someone in the pantry say about the layoffs?
qa.a: "There must be a reason. They don't cut good people."

qa.q: What did Ankita feel on hearing the pantry comment?
qa.a: Ankita felt the comforting pull of believing only mistakes get punished, but was uneasy and unconvinced, having seen Sangeeta's work.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's actions balanced support and fairness?
qa.a: Sitting with Sangeeta and writing a reference gave support, and asking in writing for the layoff criteria worked for fairness for the next list.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt when Ankita sat with her on the steps?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably felt comforted and less alone, since Ankita was not trying to explain the layoff as her fault.

grounding: Shows a person accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting a laid-off colleague and still pushing for fairness.

passage: At our school's Pongal celebration, I had to carry the pot of sweet pongal up to the stage. On the second step my slipper caught and I stumbled. The pot didn't fall, but I was sure the whole school saw. My face burned all through the kolam competition. That night I couldn't sleep. Everyone will call me "Stumble Keerthana" forever, I thought. The next morning I asked Sonali, "Did you see me fall yesterday?" She blinked. "You fell? I was so scared about my dance, I didn't see anything." I asked two more friends. One only remembered that the pongal tasted good. The other had spent the whole time looking for a lost earring. Nobody remembered the stumble at all.

qa.q: What was Keerthana carrying to the stage?
qa.a: The pot of sweet pongal.

qa.q: What was Keerthana worried about that night?
qa.a: Keerthana felt anxious and embarrassed, sure the whole school saw the stumble and would say "Stumble Keerthana" forever.

qa.q: What could Keerthana remember the next time something embarrassing happens?
qa.a: That most people are busy with their own worries, like Sonali's dance and the lost earring, and that checking with a friend can calm the fear.

qa.q: What was Sonali thinking about during the celebration?
qa.a: Sonali was busy being scared about the dance, so she didn't even notice the stumble.

grounding: Shows a child who stumbles at a school event believing everyone saw and will remember, while the others were busy with their own worries.

passage: Okay, Pranav, I'll tell you why I didn't come to the Diwali mela at school. Promise not to laugh. That morning I woke up with a huge red pimple right on my nose. Huge. I was sure everyone would stare at it the whole evening; I could already hear the jokes. Plus my kurta was last year's and a bit short. So I told Mummy I didn't feel like going, and I watched the rockets from the balcony instead. Then on Monday I looked at the photos in the class group. Nobody was looking at anybody's face; they were all crowding the food stalls. And you didn't even notice when I came back to school with the same pimple. Nobody did. So that's me, Madhav, the boy who missed the best mela of the year for one pimple.

qa.q: What did Madhav wake up with on the morning of the mela?
qa.a: A huge red pimple right on the nose.

qa.q: Why did Madhav stay home from the mela?
qa.a: Madhav was anxious and self-conscious, sure everyone would stare at the pimple and the short kurta and joke about it all evening.

qa.q: What could help Madhav the next time this worry comes up?
qa.a: Madhav could remember how the mela photos showed everyone crowding the food stalls, and go anyway, perhaps with Pranav alongside.

qa.q: What did Pranav notice when Madhav came back to school?
qa.a: Pranav didn't even notice the pimple, which shows how much smaller the audience was than Madhav imagined.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a pimple and an old kurta sure everyone will stare, who skips a school event while others barely notice.

subtype: Speaking up in class or interviews [Actor]
passage: Wasim, you keep saying you'll stay quiet in tomorrow's seminar in case you say something silly. Let me tell you about Vishal at twenty, in a freezing lecture hall in Shimla, the winter term of second year. In the first week I answered a question and said "epitome" as "epi-tome". Two people giggled. I went red and decided never to speak in that class again. And I didn't, for three whole months. I had good answers. I wrote them in the margins and swallowed them. At the end of term I asked my friend Kavita if she remembered my "epi-tome" disaster. She looked at me blankly. "When was this?" Three months of silence for a mistake nobody remembered by dinnertime. So tomorrow, you speak, hmm?

qa.q: How did young Vishal mispronounce "epitome"?
qa.a: As "epi-tome".

qa.q: Why did young Vishal stay silent for three months?
qa.a: Vishal was embarrassed and afraid the small slip would be remembered for weeks, so silence felt safer than risking another giggle.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have ended the silence sooner?
qa.a: Asking Kavita in the first week whether she remembered the slip, or simply answering one more question, would have shown that nobody was keeping track.

qa.q: How did Kavita see the "epi-tome" moment?
qa.a: Kavita didn't remember it at all, which shows others forgot the slip long before Vishal did 😅

grounding: Shows a student staying quiet for months, fearing a small slip will be remembered, while classmates forgot it almost at once.
